source.title: An Overview of Heart Rate Variability Metrics and Norms

paper.citation: Shaffer, F., & Ginsberg, J. P. (2017). An overview of heart rate variability metrics and norms. Frontiers in Public Health, 5, 258. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2017.00258
paper.abstract: What physiological processes, time-domain, frequency-domain, and nonlinear metrics, normative values, and assessment constraints should inform HRV interpretation? Participants: No original participant sample; the article summarizes prior clinical, healthy, and performance-population studies. Sport and level: Mixed populations, including athlete norm studies; no single sport or competition level. Training or return-to-play context: Resting and ambulatory HRV assessment, including performance and biofeedback contexts. Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: Narrative overview rather than a reproducible systematic review; cited norms depend on the populations and protocols of the underlying studies. Design: Narrative review and conceptual overview. Exposure or intervention: No original intervention. Comparator: HRV metrics and reference values across 24-hour, short-term (about five minutes), and ultra-short-term recordings. Measurements and outcomes: Time-domain, frequency-domain, and nonlinear HRV indices and normative values. Analysis: The authors reviewed and organized prior literature; no formal search strategy, study-selection flow, risk-of-bias assessment, or quantitative synthesis was reported.
paper.tldr: This overview provides a measurement-language reference for choosing and interpreting HRV metrics and for avoiding inappropriate comparisons across recording durations and protocols. Twenty-four-hour, short-term, and ultra-short-term HRV values are not interchangeable because recording length changes the physiological processes captured and the magnitude of time-domain indices. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Design: Narrative review and conceptual overview. Exposure or intervention: No original intervention. Comparator: HRV metrics and reference values across 24-hour, short-term (about five minutes), and ultra-short-term recordings. Measurements and outcomes: Time-domain, frequency-domain, and nonlinear HRV indices and normative values. Analysis: The authors reviewed and organized prior literature; no formal search strategy, study-selection flow, risk-of-bias assessment, or quantitative synthesis was reported.
paper.findings: Twenty-four-hour, short-term, and ultra-short-term HRV values are not interchangeable because recording length changes the physiological processes captured and the magnitude of time-domain indices. RMSSD primarily reflects beat-to-beat, vagally mediated HRV and is less affected by respiration than respiratory sinus arrhythmia, although breathing still matters for interpretation. HF power and respiratory sinus arrhythmia index vagal modulation but do not directly equal vagal tone; respiration rate and volume can substantially alter them without changing mean heart rate. The LF/HF ratio is not a simple measure of sympathovagal balance because LF power is not purely sympathetic and autonomic interactions, respiration, posture, and recording context confound interpretation. In a cited synthesis of 44 studies and 21,438 healthy adults, short-term reference means were SDNN 50 ± 16 ms and RMSSD 42 ± 15 ms, with wide study ranges and greater variation in frequency-domain indices.
paper.limitations: Ultra-short-term studies often lacked standardized protocols and explicit concurrent-validity thresholds; the authors advised against substituting ultra-short for five-minute or 24-hour values. Norms vary with device and detection method, spectral-analysis method, position, respiration, sex, age, and aerobic fitness. Higher HRV is not universally better; arrhythmia and some pathological conditions can elevate variability. Additional transfer limitation (practitioner interpretation): this narrative review is a measurement primer, not evidence that a particular HRV threshold should drive collegiate American football training decisions.
paper.practicalImplications: Standardize posture, timing, recording duration, breathing instructions, artifact handling, and metric definition before interpreting athlete trends. Prefer within-athlete longitudinal baselines matched to the same protocol; use population norms as context, not pass/fail cutoffs, and avoid interpreting LF/HF as a direct autonomic-balance score.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Standardize posture, timing, recording duration, breathing instructions, artifact handling, and metric definition before interpreting athlete trends. Prefer within-athlete longitudinal baselines matched to the same protocol; use population norms as context, not pass/fail cutoffs, and avoid interpreting LF/HF as a direct autonomic-balance score. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
